newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan coffee miller says taxes hurt growth.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan coffee miller says taxes hurt growth.

text.p: A leading Kenyan coffee miller complained on Tuesday that high taxes imposed on the industry and administered by the Coffee Board of Kenya hurt the sector.

"The coffee board deducted 1.2 billion shillings (from farmers) last year as marketing charges in 1994/95. In addition, the board deducts 3.0 percent of gross proceeds under the title ad valorem," Pius Ngugi wrote in the Daily Nation newspaper.
"The board also collects (from farmers) cess (taxes) on behalf of local authorities at the rate of 1.5 percent of gross realisation," added Ngugi, chairman of Thika Coffee Mills.

"The ad valorem levy is meant to support marketing and research. The other taxes are meant for the development and maintenance of access roads and other infrastructures in coffee growing areas." Ngugi wrote.

"The board also deducts 2.0 percent of the gross realisation as pre-emptive tax for the exchequer. This multiplicity of deductions from gross proceeds is done long before the coffee grower receives anything," Ngugi added.
Thika Coffee Mills was established with the start of coffee sector liberation in 1992. It has a licence to mill but can only export coffee after buying it at the weekly export auction.
Ngugi has in recent months joined big growers in demanding that coffee sales through the auction system be made optional.
Ngugi said a second category of deductions was effected by cooperative societies to recover loans, crop advances, farm inputs and "purported overheads" which widely varied each year.

"Usually percentages range from about 25 to 60 of the net proceeds. The poor coffee farmer ends up receiving nothing from his sweat and from the land although the original idea...was to raise income and uplift standards of living," he said.

Ngugi said although the coffee board was entrusted by the government and growers to market coffee, it had enjoyed a monopoly, illegal under the provisions of Kenya's Monopolies and restrictive Trade Act, for some 70 years.
He said in his view the board was slow to change at a time of coffee and general economic liberalisation. The board was not immediately available for comment.

Ngugi said smallholders, who account for 55 percent of total production, faced severe problems that included the rising cost of production and poor farm management which led to low yields, inefficiency in primary processing and poor quality.

Nevertheless, Coffee Board of Kenya chairman Zachariah Ngare John has persistently said a change from weekly export auctions would lead to lower quality and erosion of global confidence in Kenyan coffee. Many traders have voiced support for that view.

The board has also said it understands farm problems but its role starts only when coffee is already milled and awaiting sale at the auction. Until then, farm groups such as the Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union (KPCU) and cooperative societies had the direct responsibility of attending to grower needs.
